newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's unions urge employers to temper demands.
newsitem.headline: Spain's unions urge employers to temper demands.

text.p: Spain's unions accused employers on Monday of being inflexible in current labour reform talks, saying this endangered a deal and could prompt the government to step in and force an accord.
Unions cautioned the government at the same time to keep out of talks, warning that a forced accord would spark tension among workers.

"The position of employers to continue as before will not result in an accord....but a unilaterally imposed reform by the government that will generate unrest and undoubtedly social conflict," Antonio Gutierrez, head of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) union told a news conference.

Union and employer group leaders are due to meet on Tuesday in a last ditch attempt to reach an accord aimed at liberalising one of Europe's most rigid labour markets and preparing the economy for European Monetary Union.
The government has given unions and employers until early March to reach a deal and warned last week that it was ready to step in and impose a package of measures.
Over the weekend, the government, optimistic that a deal will be struck in time, turned down an offer from Catalan leader Jordi Pujol to mediate the talks.
"I am confident that mediation will not be necessary," Labour Minister Javier Arenas said.
"Unions and employers have asked the government not to intervene in the process and I think we must respect their independence."
However, the state's budget office director said on Monday the government intended to step in if the talks failed.
"If there is no agreement the government will create new regulations in the job market to bring us into harmony with other European countries," Jose Barea told journalists.
Spain's employers' association (CEOE) appeared certain last week that an agreement would be reached and the government would not need to interfere.
However, unions say the negotiations have come to a near standstill on a number of occasions in past weeks and the main sticking point now lies in dismissal costs.
Employers want unfair dismissal costs reduced to 25 days for each year worked with a maximum outlay of 12 months salary. Companies must currently pay 45 days for each year worked.
Some union members have begun to air doubts about employers' motives and say they are trying to provoke the government to step in.

"They are playing their cards so that the government legislates along the lines of their proposals, but this could generate social unrest," Javier Doz, spokesman for the CCOO told local media at the weekend.

Shortly after taking office, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said his priority was to reach a jobs pact with unions to help tackle Spain's unemployment, currently the worst in Europe at over 20 percent.
The previous Socialist administration took a step toward liberalising the market in 1994, introducing new specialised contracts for apprenticeships and temporary work.
But detractors say the changes institutionalised the split between permanent and temporary work, and left unresolved the issue of high dismissal costs.
